Hals.et: From Middle High German hals, from Old High German hals, from Proto-West Germanic *hals, from Proto-Germanic *halsaz.

Halskette.et: From Middle High German *halskette, from Old High German halsketinna (“neck shackle”). Equivalent to Hals (“neck”) + Kette (“chain”); cognate with Dutch halsketting.

Hals- und Beinbruch.et: Literally, “neck and leg fracture”. Probably corrupted from Yiddish הצלחה און ברכה (hatslokhe un brokhe, “success and blessing”).

halsen.et: From Middle High German halsen, from Old High German halsôn, from Proto-West Germanic *halsijan, from Proto-Germanic *halsijaną.

halsstarrig.et: From Hals + starr + -ig. Calque of Hebrew קשה ערף (Exodus 33). A biblical term similar to Swedish hårdnackad, Ancient Greek σκληροτράχηλος (sklērotrákhēlos), Russian жестоковыйный (žestokovyjnyj) etc.

Halstuch.et: From Middle High German halstuoch, from Old High German halstuoh. Equivalent to Hals + Tuch. Cognates include Dutch halsdoek.

s: a band of fabric, leather, or solid material worn around the neck: a collar, necklet, necklace
a necklace in the form of a chain
gybe (manoeuvre in which the stern of a sailing vessel crosses the wind)
the collared flycatcher (bird in the flycatcher family, Ficedula albicollis)
Halsbandschnäpper.et: Clipped compound of Halsband-Fliegenschnäpper, equivalent to Hals (“neck”) + Band (“ribbon”) + schnappen (“to catch”) + -er.

s: an affair involving a necklace, in particular: the Affair of the Diamond Necklace, an 18th-century scandal at the royal court of France
an affair involving a necklace, in particular: an affair in which Aisha, one of Muhammad’s wives, was accused of adultery
Halsbandaffäre.et: From Halsband + Affäre, a calque of French L'affaire du collier. Later applied to the Islamic episode in Orientalist literature because Aisha explained her absence from the Muslim caravan with her search for a necklace she had lost.

s: gorget (piece of armour protecting the throat; ornamental collar)
Halsberge.et: Inherited from Middle High German halsberge m or f, Old High German halsperga, from Proto-West Germanic *halsabergu, equivalent to Hals (“neck”) + bergen (“to cover”). Cognate with English hauberk.

Hals Maul.et: Literally, “neck, mouth”. A humorous reanalysis of halt's Maul.
